39: This plan describes an independent smash burger restaurant with counter service in a mid-sized American city of 150,000 to 500,000 people. The ball, a 3 oz (85 g) portion of raw beef, is smashed onto a very hot flat-top until it forms a crust, the browned, savory surface. The space is about 1,700 sq ft (158 sq m), leased as a second-generation restaurant space with a Type I hood and an exhaust duct to the roof. It has an open kitchen in view of the order counter, a self-order kiosk, {{aforo}} seats in all (tables plus a window counter) and a to-go and delivery pickup shelf by the door. Guests order at the counter or the kiosk and the food comes out on a tray at the expo, the pass where finished orders are handed off, so there are no servers. It is run by a single-owner LLC: you as owner and general manager, working the line alongside your crew. It opens in January, seven days a week from 11:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. (11:00 p.m. on Friday and Saturday), and closes on Thanksgiving, Christmas Day, New Year's Day and two maintenance days for the hood and the fryers.
40: The key figures of the example case are these. We average {{clientes_dia}} covers a day across the dining room, take-out and delivery, counting each take-out or delivery order as 1.6 covers, at an average check of {{ticket}} per cover excluding sales tax, over {{dias}} opening days. That produces {{ventas_a1}} in year-1 revenue and a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, or {{margen_neto_a1}} of sales. The average includes the ramp-up from January to April: the Excel spreads the year month by month, and Month 1 is January, one of the slower months, so the start falls on the low part of the year. Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, and cash break-even, which also covers the loan payments, is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}}. It is not a guaranteed return but a starting point: change the assumptions and enter your own numbers.
41: Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} for build-out, kitchen, refrigeration, hood, equipment and opening, which includes the security deposit and {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of rent paid before opening, plus a {{fondo_maniobra}} working capital reserve. The cash needed at opening comes to {{necesidad_caja}}. It is funded with {{fondos_propios}} of your own money ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with no interest-only period. The annual loan payment is {{cuota_anual}}. Sales tax is collected from guests and passed on to the state, so it never enters the investment.
42: From there, covers grow {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3 at the same average check, so revenue rises to {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}, and net profit to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}. The margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}} in year 1, and the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) never falls below {{dscr_min}} over the life of the loan, against the {{dscr_objetivo}} that lenders typically look for. Payback before debt comes from the cash flow in the Excel: {{payback}} with the working capital reserve counted in the investment, and {{payback_capex}} on startup costs alone.
43: You are the owner and the general manager, and you work the flat-top. With you are two grill cooks, a fry and prep cook who also builds on the make line, a shift lead who runs the order counter and the expo, counter crew who also pack to-go orders, and a weekend and evening crew: {{plantilla_puestos}} people counting you, who add up to {{plantilla_jornadas_xl}} full-time equivalents; everyone else is a W-2 employee, and how you pay yourself is a question for your CPA. The kit includes this ten-section business plan, the Burger Restaurant Financial Projections in Excel, the 80-task Burger Restaurant Startup Checklist, the Smash Burger Patty, Fries & Costing Calculator and the Equivalents Guide. What sets it apart is the cost of every ball: about 5.3 balls of 3 oz per pound and about 58.5 lb of beef a day, kit estimates that you measure yourself, plus the ground beef rule explained in plain English, with a cooking SOP of 155 °F (68 °C) for 17 seconds.
46: Not every burger restaurant is the same business, and it pays to choose before you sign anything. The ghost kitchen, or delivery-only burger brand, is a small kitchen with no dining room that lives on marketplaces. The gourmet burger bar, with servers, a thicker patty that guests order cooked to order, a higher average check and tips on top of pay, is a different business: a burger cooked to order needs the consumer advisory of Food Code 3-603.11 on the menu, and its investment looks more like a franchise. The burger truck, a smash stand on the street and at events, is the Food Truck Business Plan Kit from AI Chef Pro. Franchises and drive-thru formats need land, a larger building and a different build-out, so this plan only uses them as an investment comparison. The smash burger restaurant with counter service, a dining room, take-out and delivery is the model in this plan.
47: The value proposition is a short menu of about 14 items and a 3 oz (85 g) ball done well. The beef is a blend, a mix of cuts for the ground beef (chuck, brisket and short rib, at 80/20), smashed with a smash press, the flat steel tool, on the flat-top, the commercial steel griddle. Each burger is built on the make line, the refrigerated station where every order is assembled, on a toasted potato bun, and the fries come out with a color guide. The menu has single, double and triple smash burgers, a combo with fries and a soft drink, a crispy chicken sandwich, fries, loaded fries with cheese and bacon, and shakes. A burger on the flat-top leaves lacy edges, the thin crisp rim of the patty, and the crust that forms is what people come back for. When the order screen calls a number, the crew hands the tray over at the expo. Pickup at the restaurant is pushed with price, and the marketplace has a ceiling.
48: The menu prices to the market rather than to a wish. As a kit estimate, before sales tax, the case sells a single at $8.49, a double at $10.99, a triple at $13.49, a combo (double, fries and a soft drink) at $15.99, a crispy chicken sandwich at $10.49, fries at $3.99-4.99 and a shake at $6.49. Everything is costed ball by ball: with the kit's default values, the calculator puts a single at $2.00 of food cost, or about 24% of its price, and a double at $3.21, or about 29%. The combo comes out at about 25% and the whole week, weighted by what sells, at about 26%. The triple runs at 32.7%, the one to watch. These are estimates you measure with your own supplier, and American cheese runs about $0.14 a slice.
49: The average check in the case is {{ticket}} per equivalent cover, excluding sales tax, which is {{precio_menu}} with tax, and it comes from three channels. A dine-in guest spends about $15.00 (food $12.00 plus drinks $3.00), with the combo discount already in. A take-out order, at about $28.00 on average, is a little less than two combos, about 36 orders and 58 covers a day. A marketplace order, with the menu about 15% higher, is about $32.00 and about 19 orders and 30 covers a day. Dine-in accounts for roughly 107 covers a day. The sales mix is {{comida_pct}} food and {{bebida_pct}} beverage: drinks are about a fifth of what dine-in guests spend and a smaller share of what goes out the door.
50: One detail saves you a headache: be clear about what you are. This is a smash burger restaurant with counter service, not a full-service restaurant with a long menu, and you do not need to promise anything fancy to sell it: what counts is the crust, the toasted bun and a clean flat-top. Do not promise "gluten-free" either: the bun, the fryer and the flat-top share surfaces and utensils, and the FDA only lets you use the claim under 21 CFR 101.91. And keep "cooked to order" off the menu unless you are ready for the rules that come with it: the case cooks every smash burger through, to 155 °F (68 °C) for 17 seconds under Food Code 3-401.11(A)(2), and if you ever offer a burger cooked to order, the consumer advisory of Food Code 3-603.11 goes on your menu, your website and your marketplace listings.
53: Demand for smash burgers is better read through what people search for than through market-size estimates of doubtful origin. According to DataForSEO, on October 31, 2026 Google US shows these monthly searches: smash burger 673,000, burger restaurant 110,000 and smash burger restaurant 4,400. Read them as interest in the food, not as customers you already have. We did not find a reliable, sourced count of burger restaurants in the United States or of their average check, and that is why the plan gives neither.
54: There is a curious gap between the person who eats and the person who opens. Consumers search a lot, but the person about to open searches very little: how to start a burger business gets about 20 searches a month in the US, and burger restaurant business plan, burger business plan, how to open a burger restaurant, burger joint business plan, burger shop business plan and smash burger business get about 10 each. It is an audience that decides with data and finds almost nothing made for its case. And there is a reason to plan for delivery: a smash burger travels worse than most foods, because the crust softens in about 15 minutes, but guests now expect to order a burger for pickup or delivery from their phone, so the plan builds it in from the start.
55: On prices, a price aggregator (a weak, secondary source) puts Shake Shack's national average in May 2026 at $8.69 for the 'Shroom Burger, $4.49 for crinkle-cut fries and $6.39 for a hand-spun shake, about 20% higher in Manhattan, San Francisco and Hawaii. The case sits in that band, as a kit estimate: a single at $8.49, a double at $10.99, a combo at $15.99, fries at $3.99-4.99 and a shake at $6.49. They are references to place you, not prices to copy: check the menus in your own area. You compete on the crust, the speed and the price of the double, not on being the cheapest.
56: With Month 1 in January and in calendar order, the plan spreads sales with seasonality. February is the slowest month, with January and November next; May rises with National Burger Month and graduations; and June, July and August are the peaks, with warm weather and school out. In a college town the school year drives the curve: change the weights in the seasonality row of the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab. Month 1 in January has a consequence: the ramp-up runs from January to April, and the lowest cash balance, {{saldo_minimo}}, falls in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, which is why working capital counts.
57: The gap is clear. For how to open a burger restaurant, the Google results page (the SERP) shows an AI Overview that quotes "$30,000 to $130,000" for an independent startup, a figure that comes from a pop-up guide with no hood, next to franchise pages and forums. For burger restaurant business plan it shows class-assignment PDFs, a sample plan from an AI site and a restaurant template, and not one paid product on the first page. Nobody puts the {{capex}} of a space with a hood next to the cost of every ball, the ground beef cooking rule, or the acrylamide question in fried potatoes.
58: The demand has risks that the plan names. The price of beef moves the food cost, and the marketplace, with its commission of {{comision_pct}}, eats the margin if you let it grow above the plan's ceiling of {{plataforma_pct}} of sales. Depending on a single beef supplier is a weak point: if it fails, the flat-top fails. That is why the menu is short, pickup at the restaurant is pushed with price, and it pays to keep a second supplier on hand.
61: Before you set any price, draw a map of who competes with you in your neighborhood. In burgers, competition comes from four sides: the big fast-food chains; fast casual smash chains and full-service burger restaurants; ghost kitchens that sell only through marketplaces; and the neighborhood burger joint. Your guests are office lunches, families, students and weekend crowds, and each competitor takes them for a different reason: price, speed, convenience or nearness. With counter service there are no servers and no tips in the model: the tip jar or the POS tip belongs to the crew.
62: Porter's five forces look like this at a smash burger restaurant. Supplier power is high: ground beef depends on a few distributors, a failure shows up on the flat-top right away and the price of beef moves up and down. Customer power is high, because guests switch restaurants or apps with a click and compare prices. The threat of new entrants is high: smash is the trending format and opening looks easy, but the barrier is a space with a Type I hood and a flat-top run well. The threat of substitutes is high, with the big chains, crispy chicken sandwiches and ghost kitchens. Rivalry is intense among the smash chains and the full-service burger restaurants. Your defense is a short menu, beef bought to a written specification, costing by channel, pickup at the restaurant and a neighborhood that comes back.
63: Against a franchise, this plan is your own brand, and it pays to run both numbers. Smashburger's Item 7, the estimated initial investment of its Franchise Disclosure Document, is reported at $1,239,500-$2,255,500 and Freddy's at $785,936-$2,753,566, as reported by third-party franchise directories; check the FDD. Those ranges include real estate, the brand and the opening marketing, which an independent in a second-generation space does not carry. With your own brand, the investment is {{inversion_total}} and you keep the margin, but you also keep the risk: the menu, the beef and the flat-top depend on you. Ask any franchisor for its Franchise Disclosure Document and read Item 7 and Item 19, if it gives financial performance figures. Those figures do not transfer to a 1,700 sq ft space: compare the two accounts before you sign.
64: The barriers to entry are compliance and cash. Opening means a zoning check, plan review with the health department, a health permit and a pre-opening inspection, a building permit and a certificate of occupancy, and the hood is the filter for the space: if the building will not allow a Type I hood with UL 300 fire suppression and an exhaust duct to the roof, the flat-tops and the fryers do not fit. On top of that come the ground beef and fryer rules, which you meet with documents and records, and the investment in build-out, kitchen, refrigeration and hood. Check everything with your city, your county and your health department before you sign the lease.
65: Four factors decide whether it works. The first is the product: beef bought to a written specification, a steady crust every day and a short menu. In the kit, the usable pound of an 80/20 blend bought already ground comes to $5.41, and a pound of whole chuck to $5.15 before the labor of grinding it, so grinding in house pays off only if cleaning and grinding cost less than about $0.26 per usable lb. The second is the site: a neighborhood with lunch traffic and evening life, or a college area, foot traffic and a space with a hood. The third is cost control: the ball is the business, so every ball is weighed on a scale, never by eye, and the cost per ball and the beef yield are measured, not assumed. The fourth is the team: a grill cook and a second person who can run the flat-top.
66: The SWOT for this concept is clear. Strengths: an open kitchen, beef bought to a written specification, a short menu, costing by channel and a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}} in year 1. Weaknesses: a space with hood requirements, a flat-top that is the bottleneck of service and a cash margin of {{holgura_caja_pct}} over cash break-even that you have to protect. Opportunities: a product people search for constantly, smash as the trending format and pickup at the restaurant. Threats: the price of beef and the marketplace, where the margin on a combo falls from $12.07 dine-in to $9.12, about a quarter less. The defense is two suppliers, costing by channel and a second person who can run the flat-top.
69: The marketing strategy starts in the neighborhood and follows the calendar. You open in January, and it helps to be clear about what to expect: the curious arrive in the first month, but regulars and a good rating on the marketplaces take a quarter. That is why the plan does not count on a full dining room from day one but on a ramp. During that ramp three things matter: the flat-top in view, which explains itself from the street, a burger that comes off the line fast, and service that brings people back. Everything else is support.
70: Social media is the shop window of the flat-top, because smash burgers sell on video. Post the ball being smashed, the crust forming and the burger being built on the make line: short videos, with the smash press in your hand and the cheese melting, work better on Instagram and TikTok than menu photos. Show how to order at the counter or the kiosk, what is on each burger and when your order shows up on the screen. You do not need to post every day: a frequency you can keep is better than a burst followed by silence. And if a guest tags you in a video, ask permission before you share it.
71: Your Google Business Profile is your best free ad, because almost everyone who searches for burgers nearby looks at it, and Yelp is where many guests read before they choose. Complete both with real photos of the flat-top and the burgers, and keep the hours up to date: seven days a week, 11:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m., until 11:00 p.m. on Friday and Saturday, without forgetting the days you close, Thanksgiving, Christmas Day, New Year's Day and the two maintenance days. Answer every review, the bad ones too, calmly and in the name of the house. A careful reply reads like a commitment, and it counts for the guest who has not come yet.
72: Local acquisition starts at the door. Near a campus or an office park, the lunch rush is the simple way to fill the dining room on weekdays, with a double combo that is easy to order. Over the year the calendar gives you dates: Super Bowl Sunday and March Madness for take-out multi-packs, National Burger Month in May, graduations and summer, and football season in the fall. February is the slow month, so that is when pickup promotions earn their keep. To bring people back, keep it simple: your own ordering by phone, text or web for pickup, with no commission. There is no need to promise conversion numbers that nobody has measured.
73: Marketplace or pickup is a numbers decision. The plan sells {{plataforma_pct}} of its sales through third-party delivery marketplaces and pays a commission of {{comision_pct}} on those orders. Published plans run from 15% to 30% on DoorDash and on Uber Eats, and Grubhub has its own tiers; promotions and packaging come on top. Your own driver costs wages, employer payroll taxes and auto insurance, and in most states must be a W-2 employee, so check yours. Whatever the channel, if you ever offer a burger cooked to order, the consumer advisory goes on your listings there too.
74: Pickup at the restaurant pays no commission, so push it with price. A small discount on a pickup order costs less than the marketplace commission and brings the guest to your door, and the marketplace menu runs about 15% higher to carry its fees. There is a product problem with delivery too: a smash burger travels worse than it looks, because the crust softens in about 15 minutes, and the fries suffer most, so they go in a vented container and are fried last. That is why the ceiling of the plan is {{plataforma_pct}} of sales through marketplaces. There is no in-house delivery in the plan: if you ever set one up, do it with the numbers above in front of you.
75: The marketing budget of the case is {{marketing_anual}} a year, mostly for photography, your Google and Yelp profiles, local ads and the pickup promotions of the slow months. The brand, the website, the photos and the launch video are separate, inside the startup costs ({{inv_lanzamiento}}). Do not spend it all at once: spread the budget along the calendar and keep a part for the slower months.
